video_title: Why the Question Over How to Regulate Perps Has Turned Into a Fight
gist: A replayed RWA Summit panel (Jake Shervinsky of the Hyperliquid Policy Center, Tiffany Smith of WilmerHale, and Kathy Yun) unpacks why CME is suing the CFTC over whether perpetual futures are legally 'swaps' (institutional-only) or 'futures' (retail-accessible) — a classification fight that determines who gets US access to perps — against the backdrop of Hyperliquid's reported talks to onshore via Kraken's Bitnomial, real-world-asset perp volumes overtaking crypto-native perps, and a regulatory 'crawl-walk-run' path that panelists say makes full DeFi disintermediation impossible without an act of Congress.

themes.theme: The Core Legal Fight: Swap vs. Future Classification Determines Market Access

insights.claim: Whether a perpetual futures contract is legally classified as a 'swap' or a 'future' directly determines who can access it in the US: swaps are generally restricted to institutional participants and cannot trade on a registered designated contract market (DCM), while futures can be offered to a retail audience via a DCM — making the classification fight effectively a fight over retail access to the product.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: The outcome of this classification battle is a binary determinant of total addressable market for US perps platforms — futures classification unlocks a vastly larger retail user base than swaps classification.
insights.quote: the classification of a perpetual contract as either a swap or a future dictates whether it is only an institutional product... whereas futures are a product that can be traded by a DCM um for a retail audience.

insights.claim: The current classification confusion stems from a 'regulation by enforcement' history: five separate CFTC enforcement actions previously treated perpetuals as swaps, but when the CFTC's actual policy-setting division (not its enforcement arm) formally addressed the question for the first time, it classified perpetuals as futures — reversing the informal enforcement-driven consensus the industry had built up.
insights.speaker: Tiffany Smith
insights.so_what: Investors and builders should weight formal CFTC policy determinations far more heavily than prior enforcement-action patterns when assessing regulatory classification risk for new derivative products.
insights.quote: there were five different CFTC enforcement actions where... the CFTC took the position that pers were swaps... for the first time when you actually have... a policy setting division of the CFTC establishing how to view per they actually call it a future.

insights.claim: Jurisdiction over a given perpetual contract ultimately turns on whether its underlying asset is legally a commodity (CFTC) or a security (SEC) — the underlying asset being digital or not is not itself the relevant legal question, meaning the same classification framework will apply equally to crypto perps and real-world-asset (RWA) perps.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: RWA perps on equities, commodities, or other securities-adjacent assets will inherit the same SEC/CFTC jurisdictional battles as crypto perps, not a separate, friendlier regulatory track.
insights.quote: The question isn't whether the underlying asset is a digital asset or not. The question really is from a regulatory perspective, is the underlying asset a commodity or is it a security?

themes.theme: CME vs. CFTC: An Incumbent's Anti-Competitive Lawsuit

insights.claim: CME is suing its own regulator, the CFTC, arguing both that the process used to authorize Bitcoin perpetual futures for Coinbase and Kalshi was procedurally flawed and that the underlying determination was substantively wrong (i.e., that perpetuals are swaps, not futures) — notably, the same CFTC authorization CME is challenging would have allowed CME itself to offer the identical product.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host) / Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: The fact that CME is suing to block a product it could legally offer itself is read by panelists as revealing an anti-competitive, incumbent-protection motive rather than a genuine legal/consumer-protection concern — a red flag for how CME may respond to future competitive threats from onchain platforms.
insights.quote: The CME unfortunately disagreed even with that authorization, an authorization that would have allowed it, the CME itself to offer that exact same product, and filed a lawsuit against the CFTC.

insights.claim: CME was originally scheduled to appear on the panel to defend its position but backed out at the last minute, which panelists characterized pointedly as evasive given the company is actively litigating this exact issue in public.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: A public unwillingness to defend its legal position in front of industry peers suggests CME's litigation stance may be weaker on the merits than on competitive self-interest, worth watching as the CFTC lawsuit proceeds.
insights.quote: Originally, CME, the elephant in the room, which is perceived to be trying to do things that are anti-competitive to per was also supposed to be represented on the panel, but they backed out last minute.

themes.theme: Hyperliquid's Onshoring Path and the 'Infrastructure, Not Exchange' Framing

insights.claim: Hyperliquid was reportedly in talks with Kraken's parent company about onshoring into the US via Bitnomial, a CFTC-adjacent entity Kraken acquired, a story that broke the day before this panel and directly informed the discussion of how onchain perp platforms could gain regulated US market access.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete, near-term pathway for a major offshore/onchain perps venue to enter the regulated US market via acquisition of a licensed entity is a template other onchain platforms may replicate, and a signal of consolidation between crypto-native infrastructure and licensed US derivatives venues.
insights.quote: Bloomberg reported that Hyperlid is talking with Payword, which is the parent company of Kraken, about coming on shore through Bitnomial, which Kraken acquired.

insights.claim: The Hyperliquid Policy Center's core regulatory argument is that Hyperliquid itself is not an exchange but neutral infrastructure that any exchange can build on top of — meaning the open question for regulators is how existing exchange core-principle requirements (which assume a controlling operator) can be satisfied when the underlying settlement layer is controlled by no single party.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: If regulators accept the 'infrastructure not exchange' framing, licensed exchanges/brokers could plug into decentralized settlement layers like Hyperliquid while remaining the regulated entity — a template that could let onchain infrastructure scale within the existing regulatory perimeter rather than needing new law.
insights.quote: Hyperlid is not an exchange. Hyperlid is infrastructure that any exchange can use in order to offer the best product or service to their customers.

insights.claim: Real-world-asset (RWA) perpetuals trading volume on platforms like Hyperliquid has grown to exceed crypto-native perpetual volumes (e.g., Bitcoin perps), signaling that perps are evolving from a crypto-specific instrument into a broader multi-asset-class derivatives wrapper.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: If RWA perp volume genuinely surpasses crypto-native perp volume, the regulatory and competitive stakes of the swap-vs-future classification fight extend well beyond crypto markets into mainstream commodity/equity-adjacent derivatives — raising the addressable market materially.
insights.quote: we saw that real world asset perks really started to take off even on hyperlquid um you know the volumes of real world assets would exceed you know for instance like bitcoin perks and stuff

themes.theme: Regulatory Roadmap: 'Crawl-Walk-Run' and Why Full Disintermediation Needs Congress

insights.claim: US regulators (per Jake Shervinsky's read of CFTC leadership) are taking an incremental 'crawl walk run' approach to bringing onchain markets into the US financial system, meaning perpetual futures will initially be offered through the existing regulatory framework of licensed intermediaries using improved (onchain) technology, rather than eliminating intermediaries outright.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: Investors betting on pure DeFi disintermediation replacing licensed brokers/exchanges in the near term should recalibrate: the realistic near-term outcome is regulated intermediaries adopting onchain rails, not intermediaries disappearing.
insights.quote: What the regulators will say over and over is that they are taking a crawl walk run approach to bringing onchain markets into the US

insights.claim: A fully disintermediated market — where everyone trades directly onchain without brokers or clearinghouses — is not legally available under the current Commodity Exchange Act, which mandates that futures trade on an exchange; achieving that outcome would require Congress to amend the statute, which panelists view as extremely unlikely to happen anytime soon.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic multi-year (not multi-quarter) timeline expectation for any legislative path to pure onchain/disintermediated derivatives trading in the US, tempering more radical DeFi-maximalist market-access theses.
insights.quote: probably we would need Congress to step in and decide to amend the Commodity Exchange Act. And I hate to break it to anyone who thinks that that's on the table. That's not happening anytime soon.

insights.claim: Capitol Hill staffers and members of Congress generally do not understand that an entire onchain financial world exists that can be accessed without going through on-ramps, off-ramps, or other intermediaries — a fundamental knowledge gap shaping how crypto market-structure legislation gets written.
insights.speaker: Tiffany Smith
insights.so_what: Legislative and rulemaking outcomes on crypto market structure are likely to lag actual onchain technological capability by a wide margin, since key decision-makers lack basic conceptual familiarity with disintermediated access — a structural source of regulatory uncertainty for onchain platforms.
insights.quote: no one comprehends that there is a whole world onchain. They only think about things from an on-ramp and off-ramp perspective and they have no idea that you can access onchain the onchain world onchain activity without going through those on-ramps or other intermediaries.

themes.theme: Perpetuals as a Structurally Superior Derivative Beyond Crypto

insights.claim: Perpetual futures are argued to be structurally better than dated futures or options for many use cases because they avoid liquidity fragmentation across multiple expiration dates (yielding deeper liquidity), track the underlying asset's price more simply without needing to converge over time, and support continuous 24/7 trading — benefits already demonstrated in traditional non-crypto markets for metals like silver and gold and for oil.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: Frames perpetual futures as a genuine product-innovation threat to CME's dated-futures franchise across mainstream commodity markets (not just crypto), a structural argument for why incumbents like CME may be economically motivated to block perps regardless of their stated legal concerns.
insights.quote: They don't have fragmented liquidity across many expiration dates. So they have much deeper liquidity... these benefits have have shown themselves to be useful in markets for metals like silver and gold, in markets for oil

insights.claim: The CFTC deliberately chose to authorize perpetual futures trading on digital assets first, before evaluating other asset classes individually, specifically because physical, deliverable commodities (oil, agricultural products) have much larger real-world economic linkages — meaning a new perpetuals framework could have outsized effects on the energy industry or food supply if rolled out too quickly.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: Signals that oil and agricultural perpetual futures approval will likely lag digital-asset perps by a meaningful margin due to genuine systemic-risk considerations, not just bureaucratic caution — useful for timing expectations on when perps might expand into broader commodity markets.
insights.quote: if they allow the trading of for example oil perpetuals, what impact will that have on the energy industry? or if they were to allow the trading of perpetuals on agricultural commodities, what effect might that have on the food supply

themes.theme: Cross-Agency Turf: SEC vs. CFTC and the Event-Contract Parallel

insights.claim: The current swap/futures regulatory dichotomy is built on legal categories established by the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 (futures) and Dodd-Frank in 2010 (swaps) — both written for pre-existing financial products, not for onchain or smart-contract-based instruments — meaning some 'legal tweaks' are inevitably required to fit new products into old categories, and cross-agency inconsistency has occurred before (one past enforcement matter saw the CFTC call an asset a swap while the SEC called the same type of asset a future).
insights.speaker: Kathy Yun
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for SEC/CFTC classification conflicts on the same underlying asset type is a concrete regulatory-uncertainty risk for any RWA or crypto product that could plausibly fall under either agency's jurisdiction.
insights.quote: CFTC said an asset was a swath. SEC said it was a future, right?... you have these old categories that you're uh using for these newer assets.

insights.claim: A parallel classification battle to the perpetuals fight is already emerging in event contracts (prediction markets) — e.g., whether a contract resolving on a future stock price should be an SEC-regulated security-based derivative versus one resolving on a company's reported earnings or output — illustrating that the swap/future/security line-drawing problem is a generic feature of nearly all novel derivative products, not unique to perpetuals or onchain markets.
insights.speaker: Jake Shervinsky
insights.so_what: Investors and builders in the prediction-market space should expect the same multi-year classification uncertainty currently playing out in perps to affect event contracts, making regulatory clarity timing a shared risk across both product categories.
insights.quote: Questions like if you have an event contract based on what price a stock will be at a given time, should the SEC regulate that as a securitybased derivative?... it's hard to draw the line

insights.claim: The industry's proposed fix is a bespoke, risk-based disclosure and classification framework tailored to how a given product actually functions (citing the SEC's 'Reg Crypto' tailored-disclosure proposal as a positive precedent) rather than reflexively applying old Dodd-Frank-era swap rules — which were both over-inclusive (imposing compliance requirements that don't fit) and under-inclusive (missing genuinely novel, smart-contract-specific risks) when applied to fundamentally new products.
insights.speaker: Tiffany Smith
insights.so_what: Argues for a specific policy design principle — purpose-built, activity-based rules rather than retrofitted legacy categories — that investors evaluating regulatory tailwinds/headwinds for onchain derivatives platforms should watch for in future CFTC/SEC rulemaking.
insights.quote: trying to strap on regulation that wasn't fit for purpose and sort of missing out on the risks here... it's both overincclusive... and underinclusive because it's not asking the right riskbased smart contract based types of questions.
